articles.title: Building a local handwriting font workshop with editable glyphs
articles.excerpt: I built GlyphSprout for projects that need a small set of personal characters. It turns a handwritten page into a font subset that I can inspect and adjust one glyph at a time. The workflow begins wit…
articles.body: I built GlyphSprout for projects that need a small set of personal characters. It turns a handwritten page into a font subset that I can inspect and adjust one glyph at a time. The workflow begins with an A4 template. Each page has 35 cells, and a project can use up to 512 supported BMP characters across 15 pages. The input is a flat, evenly lit PNG or JPEG scan. I assign the page, confirm its visible ID, and place four registration corners by hand. GlyphSprout shows a rectified preview and asks me to confirm the page before worker processing starts. The tracing step thresholds each cell and removes small connected specks. It follows the black ink as independent contours, so counters and detached dots remain part of the glyph. I keep the source cell visible beside the outline.

articles.body: Ouço muito a pergunta "EventBridge ou SQS?". Quase sempre ela está mal formulada. Na maioria dos fluxos com mais de um consumidor, os dois trabalham juntos: o EventBridge decide para onde o evento vai, e o SQS segura esse evento até alguém poder processar. Roteamento e durabilidade são problemas diferentes, então um não substitui o outro. Este artigo mostra onde cada peça entra, o que cada uma resolve sozinha e quais erros aparecem quando alguém usa as duas sem saber por quê. 1.0 O que cada serviço realmente resolve Os dois aparecem juntos em quase toda discussão porque ambos recebem mensagens. Mas o trabalho de cada um é diferente: o EventBridge decide para onde a informação vai, e o SQS guarda a informação até alguém processá-la. 1.1 EventBridge O EventBridge é um barramento de eventos.

articles.title: Label your form fields: a two-minute check before you ship
articles.excerpt: Forms are where landing pages make or lose a signup, and a missing label is one of the easiest problems to ship without noticing. It looks fine. Everything works with a mouse. But a screen reader user…
articles.body: Forms are where landing pages make or lose a signup, and a missing label is one of the easiest problems to ship without noticing. It looks fine. Everything works with a mouse. But a screen reader user lands on a box that says "edit text" and has to guess. This is a two-minute check you can run on any form. What a label actually does According to MDN, a label is not only visually next to its input. It is programmatically associated with it, so a screen reader reads the label out when the input gets focus. It also gives you a bigger target: clicking or tapping the label passes focus to the input, which helps on touch screens. So a label is both an accessibility feature and a usability one. The check Click the label text. Does the cursor land in the field?

articles.title: How I Batch-Stamp and Rename 40 Invoices in One Go
articles.excerpt: Every month, my clients' suppliers send me a folder's worth of invoices as PDFs. The filenames are chaos: INV_final2.pdf, scan0003.pdf, document (1).pdf. Before any of them can go to the bookkeeper, e…
articles.body: Every month, my clients' suppliers send me a folder's worth of invoices as PDFs. The filenames are chaos: INV_final2.pdf , scan0003.pdf , document (1).pdf . Before any of them can go to the bookkeeper, each one needs two things: a "RECEIVED" stamp with the date, and a filename a human can search later — my pattern is YYYY-MM-DD_vendor_total.pdf . Doing this by hand for ~40 files took me about an hour of opening, stamping, saving, renaming. Now the mechanical part is a script, and my job is a 10-minute review pass. Here's the setup, including the parts that broke. The pipeline Three folders: inbox/ (originals, never touched), work/ (script output), review/ (files the script couldn't handle, which I fix manually).

articles.title: Your User Closed the Tab. Your Node Server Is Still Paying for the LLM Call
articles.excerpt: Book: AI That Ships The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claud…
articles.body: Book: AI That Ships The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub Your user asks the support bot for a full migration plan. Three seconds in, they see the answer is going the wrong way and close the tab. The browser drops the connection. Your Node handler doesn't notice. It keeps pulling tokens off the model stream, keeps writing them into a socket nobody is reading, and when the model asks for a tool call, it runs the tool and sends the whole conversation back for another turn. Nothing crashed, so nothing alerted. The only trace is on the invoice. Node doesn't cancel any of this for you.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 13, 1773: Astronomer Charles Messier discovers the Whirlpool Galaxy before we ever knew it was a galaxy
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the "Whirlpool Galaxy," also known as Messier 51, or M51. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 13, 1773, a French astronomer named Charles Messier discovered the " Whirlpool Galaxy , " also known as Messier 51, or M51. Charles Messier was scanning the sky for objects that could confuse comet hunters when he catalogued the galaxy as M51. However, Messier wasn't able to see the spiral structure, and he didn't identify it as a galaxy. Seventy-two years later, another astronomer named William Parsons saw the whirlpool shape, but he thought it was a spiral nebula. Eventually, Edwin Hubble found out that M51 and other features like it were actually galaxies. Spiral galaxy M51 (NGC 5194), The Whirlpool Galaxy, displays its long arms which consist of stars and gas laced with dust arranged in long lanes, in this view from the Hubble Space Telescope.

articles.title: Earth's poles shifted surprisingly fast during the age of dinosaurs, ancient sea levels reveal
articles.excerpt: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander.
articles.body: The location of Earth's geographic poles has changed several times over the past 320 million years in a process known as true polar wander, according to measurements of ancient flooding brought about by sea level changes resulting from our planet's crust shifting relative to Earth's spin axis. Such a shift can affect climate, both on local scales and globally, as regions that were by the poles find themselves moving down to lower latitudes and vice versa. This can then affect atmospheric circulation patterns, which affect climate across the world. The changes would have affected the environments in which life developed and evolved, from the age of the dinosaurs through to some of our oldest primate ancestors.

articles.title: SpaceX rocket launch creates incredible 'space jellyfish' visible throughout US East Coast (photos)
articles.excerpt: The SpaceX cargo launch to the International Space Station on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13) created a dazzling display seen up and down the US East Coast.
articles.body: Rockets are launching to space on a near-daily basis these days, but short of livestreaming a liftoff from the comfort of your Wi-Fi router, relatively few spectators are in the right place and time to see one with their own eyes. That wasn't the case Tuesday morning (Oct. 13), when SpaceX launched the CRS-35 mission for NASA . A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Pad 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida at 6:35 a.m. EDT (1035 GMT), carrying a cargo variant of SpaceX's Dragon spacecraft on the company's 35th commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station (ISS). Following the northward path of the space station's orbit at the time, the rocket flew a trajectory along the United States' East Coast.
